To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

IL-13 induced production of mucus in human bronchus tissue and release of inflammatory mediators in human lung tissue but did not induce airways hyperresponsiveness in human and non-human primate lung tissue.
IL-13 induced mucus secretion in human lung tissue and that anti-IL-13 treatment attenuated IL-13 induced secretion of mucin5Ac and inflammatory cytokines in human lung tissue.
IL-13 induced allergic inflammation in human bronchus and bronchiole tissue but did not induce airways hyperresponsiveness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel anti-asthmatics and the development of human relevant models for their evaluation.
the development of targeted therapies for the treatment of severe asthma.
the development of new therapeutic approaches in asthma and COPD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IL-13 induces allergic inflammation in human lungs, which can be attenuated by anti-IL-13 and anti-IL-4Ra treatment.
human PCLS represent a valuable model to evaluate the effect of IL13 in human lungs.
human PCLS are a valuable tool to assess efficacy and safety of new therapies for asthma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human PCLS model can serve as a translational tool for the assessment of anti-inflammatory drugs.
IL-13 induces allergic inflammation and mucus secretion in human lung tissue, however, no AHR was observed.
IL-13 induced mucus and biomarker release but no airway constriction in human lung tissue, which was in contrast to rodents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the IL-13 pathway may represent a promising target for novel asthma treatments.
IL-13 induces allergic inflammation and mucus production but does not induce airway constriction in human lung tissue.
human tissue can be used to test the efficacy of anti-IL-13 therapies and the results obtained can be translated into the clinic.
